# Context

- Today: make 11 substantive decisions (~5 min each)
- Rest is wording/clarification, handled as offline drafting

- Batch 2 ongoing
- Batch 3 starting next week (delayed)
- \~2500 patients included.

# The 11 decisions

1. Interim analysis vs routine trial monitoring (p. 13)
2. Length-of-stay: counts, durations, or time-to-event? (pp. 16, 18, 21, 26)
3. Intercurrent-events table (pp. 18–21)
4. Missing data (pp. 27–28)

# 1. Is "Interim analysis" really trial monitoring (§4.5, p. 13)

**Decision:** terminology, and what the half-way report contains.

- The document calls the half-way review an "interim analysis", but nothing in §4.5 is a stopping rule based on the treatment effect. The per-batch reports are really routine trial monitoring.

**Suggestion:**

- Call per batch summaries **"routine monitoring reports"**
- Call the half-way report **"interim analysis"** (included in protocol).
- Ask for a decision to continue or stop half-way.
- Exclude outcome comparisons and formal effect-based stopping rules.

# 2. Length-of-stay: counts, durations, or time-to-event? (§9.2.5–9.2.8, pp. 16, 18, 21, 26)

**Decision:** statistical model, effect measure, estimand wording (ED, hospital, ICU LOS).

- LOS is analysed with negative binomial regression, but the data are recorded as **date and time** (continuous durations).
- Options:
  - **gamma/log-link** reporting a ratio of expected LOS
  - **time-to-event** with death as a competing risk; either way the estimand (observed duration until exit) should be stated and

**Suggestion:**

- State the estimand as observed duration until exit an prefer the gamma/log-link model.
- Interpret alongside mortality and transfer frequencies.

# 3. Intercurrent-events table: what belongs there? (§8.1, pp. 18–21)

**Decision:** restructure Table 1 / simplify §8.1.

- The table currently mixes three different things: true intercurrent events, missing-data issues (loss to follow-up, outcomes that cannot be ascertained), and an outcome definition (ICU admission only if admission precedes death/transfer).

**Suggestion:**

- Remove loss to follow up from the list of intercurrent events
- Remove ICU outcome definition as well
- Add "treatment policy" wording (exposure already follows the scheduled transition date)

::: notes
Timebox 4 min. This has broad consensus in the comments; it mostly needs an in-room "yes" and owner AO.
:::

# 4. Missing data: replace the 10% rule? (§9.4, pp. 27–28)

**Decision:** primary estimator, role of multiple imputation, imputation specification.

- The 10%-missing threshold is arbitrary: bias depends on the missingness mechanism.

**Suggestion:**

- drop the 10% fixed-threshold framing
- pre-specify primary analysis as using all available observed outcome data
- use multiple imputation as a sensitivity analysis under a MAR assumption
- consider missingness separately for each outcome

::: notes
Timebox 7 min. Two clean options: available-cases primary + MI sensitivity, or always prespecified MI. Pick one and decide the tipping-point question.
:::

# 5. Adjust the primary model for randomisation factors? (§9.1, pp. 23, 27)

**Decision:** include the cluster-size randomisation variable as a fixed covariate?

- Randomisation is covariate-constrained on anticipated cluster size, but the primary model does not adjust for it (it adjusts for time and cluster random effects only).

**Suggestion:** include anticipated cluster size as a fixed covariate (adjusting for randomisation factors is a reviewer expectation) and make the cluster + cluster-by-period random effects explicit in the text.

::: notes
Timebox 4 min. Randomisation-factor adjustment is a reviewer expectation, so the default is to add cluster size. Only argue the alternative if model complexity genuinely threatens convergence (see the small-sample discussion).
:::

# 6. Small-sample inference & model-fit criteria (§9, pp. 23, 27)

**Decision:** pre-specified wording for corrections and acceptable fit.

- The SAP needs a pre-specified small-sample correction for the non-linear models (the choice affects SEs, CIs and p-values and must not be data-driven), plus criteria for acceptable fit beyond convergence.

**Suggestion:**

- Kenward–Roger for linear models and an objective fallback for GLMMs (the t(K−2) convention has worked well with few clusters)
- accept zero variance components (simpler structures as sensitivity)
- keep randomisation at hospital level, no unit-level random effect.

::: notes
Timebox 4 min. This is wording plus a modelling convention; the t(K−2) and zero-variance guidance are strong defaults. The unit-level question deserves a quick yes/no here.
:::

# 7. QoL & disability: separate or longitudinal? (§9.2.2–9.2.3, p. 25)

**Decision:** per-time-point analyses, or one joint longitudinal model?

- QoL and disability are measured at several post-discharge time points and the current text implies separate per-time-point analyses.

**Suggestion:** one **joint longitudinal model**, with time, time×treatment interaction and patient-level random effects, reporting the effect at each time point from the model.

::: notes
Timebox 4 min. There is a clear methodological preference for the joint longitudinal model; expect a quick decision.
:::

# 8. Effect sizes: odds ratio, risk ratio, or marginal effect? (§8.4, §9.1, pp. 22–24)

**Decision:** the effect measure each outcome reports:

- We currently state that we will estimate both the OR and the ARD. Should we change this to reporting RR?
- The adherence proportion is reported as a logit-scale difference; an average marginal effect (the difference in expected percentage of checklist items completed) is easier to communicate.

**Suggestion:**

- Keep OR and ARD
- For adherence, report the **average marginal effect** as a difference in expected percentage points.
- Before finalising, clarify what "get Res on these" refers to (KH?)

::: notes
Timebox 4 min. Two threads: (1) JK's preference for risk ratios for binary outcomes, (2) adopting the average marginal effect for the adherence proportion. Settle the reporting principle once per outcome type; the open thread is comment 155, ask KH today if possible.
:::

# 9. Sensitivity analyses (§9.5, pp. 28–30)

**Decision:** the final list of sensitivity analyses, consistent with the protocol.

- The list is long and a prior paper was criticised for too many sensitivity analyses.

**Currently specified analyses:**

| Sensitivity analysis | In the protocol? |
|---|---|
| 9.5.1 Exposure by actual transition date | No (SAP addition) |
| 9.5.2 Autoregressive within-cluster correlation | Yes |
| 9.5.3 Random cluster × intervention | Yes |
| 9.5.4 Time modelled with a spline | Yes |
| 9.5.5 Lag & weaning effects | Yes |
| Multiple imputation under MAR | No (SAP missing-data plan) |

**Suggestion:**

- keep the analyses to avoid a major protocol amendment.

::: notes
Timebox 5 min. Four of the five analyses are mandated by the protocol (9.5.2–9.5.5); only 9.5.1 is an SAP addition. Agree on 9.5.1 (keep or drop). Flag that cutting any protocol-mandated analysis requires a protocol amendment.
:::

# 10. Subgroups: age groups & geographical region (§9.7, pp. 30–31)

**Decision:** age categorisation; how the primary subgroup is handled.

- Four age groups risk some subgroups with very few events and the expected patient distribution is unknown.
- The final set of states (geographical region) is not fixed, yet region is currently the primary subgroup.

**Suggestion:**

- use two clinically justified age groups (cut-off fixed before analysis)
- for region, use zonal councils (Northern, Southern, Central, Eastern, Western, North Eastern)

::: notes
Timebox 5 min. Give the age-distribution question priority; nothing is decided on age until we have the expected distribution.
:::

# 11. Can a patient appear more than once? (§9, p. 30)

**Decision:** inclusion rule for repeated ED presentations; any within-patient correlation modelling.

- A patient can present to the ED more than once, but the models only include cluster-level random effects.

**Suggestion:** treat multiple presentations as independent because they are expected to be rare (alternative is to include only the first presentation per patient)

::: notes
Timebox 3 min. Default is the first-presentation rule unless re-presentation is common.
:::
